Informal adjudication may appear to involve an obvious trade-off— 
flexibility, simplicity, and lower decision making costs in exchange for 
greater risk that unconstrained, unaccountable officials will make 
arbitrary decisions. In the national security domain, for example, section 
215 of the USA Patriot Act, Pub. L. No. 107-56 (Oct. 26, 2001), allows the 
FBI to make highly discretionary decisions about whether to obtain 
business records without a subpoena to further counter-intelligence or 
counter-terrorism investigations. Agency actions involving priorities for 
immigration investigation or the issuance of occupational safety 
compliance orders also leave agencies enormous substantive and practical 
discretion. It may seem obvious that this discretion is in greater danger of 
being abused because it is relatively free from procedural regulation. But 
this oversimplification neglects several less obvious sources of constraint 
on informal adjudication.
First, even for adjudication subject to no statutory procedural 
requirements, the availability of judicial review may help to mitigate the 
potential risks of excessive discretion even as it reduces some of the 
advantages of informality. See, e.g.. Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp. v. LTV 
Corp., 496 U.S. 633 (1990); Indep. U.S. Tanker Owners Comm. v. Lewis, 
690 F.2d 908 (D.C. Cir. 1982). An agency that appears to have unfettered 
procedural discretion will still be constrained by the need to generate a 
sufficient record for judicial review. This is because “[t]he APA specifically 
contemplates judicial review on the basis of the agency record compiled in 
the course of informal agency action in which a hearing has not occurred.” 
Florida Power & Light Co. v. Lorion, 470 U.S. 729, 744 (1985).
Second, institutional forces constrain discretionary decisions by 
agency personnel. These forces include the incentives and supervision of 
adjudicative officials, non-judicial forms of oversight within the executive 
branch and by Congress, and the mission and culture of the agency in 
question. Audits and other techniques of statistical quality assurance can 
also help to ensure the consistency and quality of otherwise unreviewed or 
unreviewable informal decision making. See Mariano-Florentino Cuellar, 
Auditing Executive Discretion, 82 NOTRE DAME L. REV. 227 (2006). For an 
argument that such systems should be considered an essential aspect of 
administrative due process, see Jerry L. Mashaw, The Management Side of 
Due Process: Some Theoretical and Litigation Notes on the Assurance of 
Accuracy, Fairness and Timeliness in the Adjudication of Social Welfare
